title: Only 7% Pass This Obsolete Items Quiz
summary: Pagers, cassette tapes, floppy disks and other everyday relics test how well you remember life before smartphones.

landing.intro: From pagers and rabbit-ear antennas to floppy disks and film cameras, see how many things from the past you still remember.

about.body:
This quick worldwide-English picture quiz revisits ten objects and habits that were once part of everyday life. The challenge moves through communication, home entertainment, photography, storage and navigation without relying on specialist historical knowledge.

The photographs are used with permission, and the questions retain the source quiz’s familiar recognition-and-usage style. Look closely at the controls, shapes and surroundings before choosing from the four possible answers.

Your final percentage reflects this entertainment challenge only. Some objects remain in occasional or specialist use, so “obsolete” describes their disappearance from ordinary daily life rather than claiming that every example has vanished completely.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Inspect each photograph and read the short question about the object or how it was used.
Choose one of four answers. Correctness stays hidden until the final result.
Finish all ten pictures to reveal your Obsolete Objects Score and review every missed answer.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. Product names belong to their respective owners, and this quiz is not a formal history assessment.

details.analysisTitle: How to read your retro score
details.analysisCopy: This ten-picture result combines communication devices, home entertainment, film photography, data storage and old navigation habits. Each correct answer moves the headline percentage by ten points.
details.roadmapIntro: Your score is the first signal. Continue through the report to see which parts of everyday retro life felt most familiar and review every missed item.

details.measuredIntro: The ten selected photographs span five broad parts of pre-smartphone daily life.

measuredAreas.title: Communication and entertainment
measuredAreas.copy: Recognising pagers, telephones, television equipment and portable audio habits.

measuredAreas.title: Film photography
measuredAreas.copy: Remembering darkrooms, disposable cameras and the physical process behind printed photographs.

measuredAreas.title: Storage and navigation
measuredAreas.copy: Identifying floppy disks and the paper-based tools people relied on before cloud storage and map apps.

details.tipsTitle: Three ways to identify obsolete objects
details.tipsIntro: Use these clues if you attempt the picture challenge again.

tips.title: Look for physical controls
tips.copy: Rotary dials, tape reels, tuning rods and large mechanical buttons often reveal the object’s era and purpose.

tips.title: Notice what replaced it
tips.copy: Thinking about the modern phone, app or digital service that performs the same job can lead you back to the older object.

tips.title: Read the surroundings
tips.copy: A classroom screen, car glove box or photo-processing setup can be as important as the object itself.

questions.question: Before smartphones, people carried this device to receive short numeric messages. What is it?

image.alt: A small black electronic device with a narrow display and several buttons

questions.explanation: A pager, also called a beeper, received short numeric messages. The recipient would then find a telephone and call the displayed number.

questions.question: What was the primary purpose of a pencil when used with a cassette tape like this?

image.alt: A clear audio cassette with a pencil inserted through one of its reel openings

answers: To manually rewind or fix tangled tape
To stop the tape from playing
questions.explanation: A pencil fitted into the cassette reel and could be turned to rewind loose tape or carefully pull tangled tape back into the shell.

questions.question: What were these “rabbit ears” found on top of old television sets used for?

image.alt: Two long metal aerial rods extending upward from an old television set

questions.explanation: Rabbit ears were an indoor television antenna. Adjusting the two rods could improve reception of over-the-air broadcast signals.

questions.question: In the era of film photography, why was a red light used in a darkroom?

image.alt: A photographic darkroom illuminated by a dim red safety light

answers: To make the room look cool
To signal that the door was locked
To develop photos without exposing light-sensitive paper
questions.explanation: A darkroom safelight used a wavelength that suitable black-and-white photographic paper was less sensitive to, allowing prints to be handled during processing.

questions.question: How did you “dial” a number on this type of vintage telephone?

image.alt: A black telephone with a circular numbered finger wheel

answers: By rotating the finger wheel for each digit
By sliding a lever up and down
questions.explanation: A rotary telephone used a circular finger wheel. Each digit was turned to a stop and released before the next digit was entered.

questions.question: What was the purpose of this small plastic floppy disk before USB drives existed?

image.alt: Three square magnetic computer disks in different sizes and colours

answers: To store and transfer digital files
questions.explanation: Floppy disks were removable magnetic storage. People used them to save and move documents, programs and other relatively small files.

questions.question: What did you have to do to a disposable camera after taking all the photos?

image.alt: A simple single-use film camera with a fixed lens, flash and winding control

answers: Turn the whole camera in to a shop for developing
Press a Print button on the back
questions.explanation: The exposed film stayed inside a disposable camera, so the complete camera was handed to a photo shop or laboratory for processing.

questions.question: Before Google Maps, what did people keep in their car’s glove box to find their way?

image.alt: A closed glove compartment built into the dashboard of a car

questions.explanation: Drivers commonly kept a paper road atlas or folded maps in the glove box and planned routes by following printed roads and place names.

questions.question: What was this overhead projector used for in classrooms?

image.alt: A classroom overhead projector casting the image of a transparent sheet onto a screen

answers: Shining light through transparent sheets onto a wall
questions.explanation: An overhead projector shone light through a transparent sheet and used a lens and mirror to enlarge the image onto a wall or screen.

questions.question: What is this device that allowed people to listen to music on the go using cassette tapes?

image.alt: A portable Sony music player beside a pair of earphones

questions.explanation: The original Sony Walkman popularised private portable listening with compact cassette tapes and lightweight headphones.
